name: Megavitamin therapy

lead: Megavitamin therapy is the practice of taking vitamins in amounts far above dietary recommendations, often tens or hundreds of times higher. It grew out of orthomolecular medicine, a 1960s movement associated with Linus Pauling, Abram Hoffer and Humphry Osmond, which holds that the right concentrations of natural substances can correct disease and support health. People who follow high-dose regimens generally hope for broader wellbeing, including clearer skin, healthier hair and more energy, which is how it connects to appearance.

Research is mixed by vitamin and condition. Controlled trials in attention disorders and psychiatric conditions did not find benefit, and professional bodies such as the American Psychiatric Association have criticised the broad claims. Narrow medical uses exist, such as niacin for lipid disorders or vitamin supplementation for specific inherited metabolic conditions, under clinical supervision.

paras: Practitioners of orthomolecular medicine typically combine blood tests and symptom histories with individualised high-intake plans of vitamins, minerals and amino acids, sometimes including intravenous vitamin C. Online, people describe stacking single-nutrient supplements (vitamin C, B-complex, niacin, vitamin A or D) well beyond label amounts, usually alongside diet changes. Reported time frames are weeks to months.

Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) accumulate and can reach toxic levels; excess vitamin A is linked to birth defects and liver harm, and long-term high vitamin B6 causes nerve damage. High-dose niacin can cause flushing and liver enzyme elevation, and high vitamin C can raise uric acid excretion and kidney-stone risk. Reviews advise that people with specific deficiencies, absorption problems or medical conditions should work with a clinician, and that supplements are not a replacement for treatment.

angle.text: Practitioners say that saturating the body with vitamins supports whole-body health, and people pursuing appearance goals often include skin, hair and nail benefits among the hoped-for results. Trial evidence is mixed by vitamin and condition, and several vitamins carry toxicity limits.

lead: Megavitamin therapy is the use of vitamins at doses far above recommended dietary allowances, commonly 10 to 100 times higher or more, in the hope of producing a therapeutic effect rather than just preventing deficiency [1][2]. It is the practical arm of orthomolecular medicine, a school of thought that treats disease and promotes health by adjusting the concentrations of naturally occurring substances in the body [2].

For people interested in appearance, the appeal is a chain: higher vitamin intake is expected to support general health, skin quality, hair, nails and energy, which in turn show up in how someone looks. Skin, hair and nail goals are common reasons for taking individual vitamins, and megavitamin regimens extend the same reasoning to larger amounts.

The practice originated in the 1950s with the psychiatrists Abram Hoffer and Humphry Osmond, who gave high-dose niacin to people with schizophrenia, and was broadened by Linus Pauling's 1968 description of orthomolecular psychiatry [1][2]. Controlled trials and professional reviews have generally not supported the broad claims, and toxicity from some vitamins at high intakes is well documented [3][4].
infobox: Supplements sold freely; practice not endorsed by major medical bodies

paras: Megavitamin therapy means taking a vitamin or several vitamins at intakes many times above the recommended daily allowance. Proponents aim for pharmacological effects, such as saturating enzyme systems or acting as antioxidants, rather than correcting a diet-related shortfall [1]. It differs from ordinary multivitamin use, which supplies amounts close to the recommended intake.

The idea sits within orthomolecular medicine, whose supporters say the standard allowances only prevent deficiency diseases and that illness reflects a need for higher or individually tailored nutrient levels [2]. Practitioners often use blood tests and personal histories to design regimens containing vitamins, minerals, amino acids and fatty acids [2].

By the 1930s some physicians were prescribing large vitamin doses for disease, and in 1948 William McCormick began using high-dose vitamin C; Fred Klenner followed in the 1950s [2]. In the 1950s Abram Hoffer and Humphry Osmond reported on high-dose niacin for schizophrenia, with a paper in 1957, and the term megavitamin became attached to the approach [2][1].

Linus Pauling used the term orthomolecular in a 1968 paper in Science and became the movement's best-known advocate, promoting high-dose vitamin C and other nutrients for a range of conditions including infections and cancer [1][2]. The Journal of Orthomolecular Medicine began in 1967 under its earlier name, the Journal of Schizophrenia [2].

Proponents hold that disease reflects a lack of the body's optimal nutritional environment and that individualised high intakes correct imbalances [2]. Claimed applications include schizophrenia, autism, hyperactivity, heart disease, the common cold and cancer [1][2]. Hoffer said the approach was not meant to replace standard treatment [2].
In appearance-focused communities, high-dose vitamins are discussed as a way to improve skin, hair and nails and to boost energy for training, usually as part of broader supplement stacks.

A 1984 randomised, double-blind crossover trial of a megavitamin regimen (niacinamide, ascorbic acid, calcium pantothenate and pyridoxine) in 41 children with attention deficit disorders found no significant difference from placebo on most behaviour scores, and 42% of participants exceeded upper limits for serum transaminases while taking the vitamins [3]. A 1977 JAMA article reviewing megavitamins for minimal brain dysfunction described it as a potentially dangerous therapy [4].

A 1973 American Psychiatric Association task force reviewed the orthomolecular literature and judged the proponents' evidence unconvincing; the American Academy of Pediatrics criticised the approach in 1976 [2]. A 1984 review of vitamin safety noted that a well-balanced diet supplies vitamins adequately in healthy people and that supplements are suggested mainly for inadequate intake, absorption problems or increased needs [5].

Narrow uses are accepted in medicine: niacin for lipid disorders and high-dose vitamins for some rare inborn errors of metabolism [2]. Large trials of vitamin E have not shown clear benefit, and several meta-analyses linked supplementation to higher mortality, though one later analysis did not [2].

Reviews describe toxicity from excess fat-soluble vitamins and vitamin A in particular, including effects on development in pregnancy [5][6]. Chronic high intake of pyridoxine (vitamin B6) is associated with nerve damage, and animal work shows protein-deficient diets can enhance the neurotoxicity [7]. High-dose vitamin C increases uric acid excretion in human studies [8]. Other reported risks include liver toxicity from niacin, hypertension, kidney stones and forgoing conventional care [2].

In South Africa, vitamin products promoted by Matthias Rath as AIDS treatments were linked by the South African Medical Association to several deaths, and the Cape High Court declared his unauthorised trials unlawful [2].

Controlled human trials of megavitamin regimens are mostly from the 1980s and focus on attention deficit disorders: the 1984 crossover trial found no benefit over placebo and noted elevated liver enzymes [3], and a 1992 review of trials reached a similar question on ADHD [9]. A study of 14 people found 4 grams of ascorbic acid markedly increased uric acid clearance [8]. No trial in these sources tested megavitamin regimens for skin, hair or other appearance outcomes.

lore.intro: Megavitamin ideas circulate through orthomolecular medicine and supplement culture; people interested in looks tend to apply them to skin, hair and energy.
